subject: Archaeology
title: Isotope Analysis: You Are What You Eat
description: A quick, practical guide to Isotope Analysis: You Are What You Eat.

hook.text: Your bones record what you ate and where you grew up. Ancient skeletons carry the same chemical autobiography.

buildup.text: Strontium isotopes in tooth enamel match the geology of where a person grew up.

discovery.text: Carbon and nitrogen isotopes in bone reveal diet. High nitrogen means meat-heavy diets; high carbon-13 means marine food.

twist.text: The Amesbury Archer, found near Stonehenge, grew up in the Alps. He traveled 800 miles to England 4,000 years ago.

climax.text: Isotope analysis is rewriting migration history. People moved far more often in prehistory than anyone assumed.

punchline.text: Your teeth remember where you were born. Archaeology just learned to read them.

quiz.question: What did isotope analysis reveal about the Amesbury Archer?
options: He had a diet entirely of seafood despite living inland
He grew up in the Alps and traveled 800 miles to Stonehenge
He was the oldest known resident of Britain

details.summary: Isotope analysis of bones and teeth reveals what ancient people ate, where they grew up, and where they traveled. Strontium isotopes reflect geological origin, carbon isotopes distinguish plant-based diets, and nitrogen isotopes indicate meat consumption and breastfeeding patterns.
details.whyItMatters: Isotope analysis turns skeletons into biographical records. It can determine whether a person was local or immigrant, whether they ate seafood or grain, and even when they were weaned as infants — all from chemical signatures in bones.
takeaways: Strontium isotopes reveal where a person grew up geographically
Carbon isotopes distinguish between different plant food sources
Nitrogen isotopes indicate protein intake and breastfeeding history

faq.question: How can isotopes tell where someone grew up?
faq.answer: Strontium isotope ratios vary by local geology. Tooth enamel forms in childhood and locks in the local strontium signature. Comparing tooth enamel to local geological values reveals whether a person grew up locally or migrated from a region with different geology.

faq.question: What dietary information can isotope analysis provide?
faq.answer: Carbon-13 ratios distinguish between C3 plants like wheat and C4 plants like maize. Nitrogen-15 levels increase up the food chain, so high values indicate a meat-rich or marine diet. Combined, these isotopes reconstruct detailed dietary patterns across populations and time periods.
